deep.reconstruction:
This page is a printed proof sheet (p. 8) of Riemann's posthumous paper 'Mechanik des Ohres', published by Henle in 1867. It continues the argument begun on p. 7. That argument establishes the extreme sensitivity of the middle-ear apparatus (thesis I). It uses Nicholson's report that sentries' calls at Portsmouth are heard 4-5 English miles away at Ryde.

(a) Recap from p. 7, needed here. Assume intensity (mechanical force, i.e. energy flux) falls off as I ∝ 1/r^2, or faster. Amplitude A satisfies A ∝ sqrt(I) ∝ 1/r. Taking r2/r1 ≈ 2000 (4-5 miles against 8-10 ft):
- I1/I2 ≈ 2000^2 = 4·10^6;
- A1/A2 ≈ 2000.

(b) Psychophysical justification (top of page). Our sensation of loudness does not show ratios like 1:10^6. Riemann says this is no objection. The relation between felt and physical intensity is presumably like that between the estimated brightness (magnitude) of fixed stars and the mechanical force of their light. There, photometry and star gauges show that the physical intensity decreases geometrically as magnitude increases arithmetically. In modern terms this is m − m0 = −k·log(I/I0), i.e. the Weber–Fechner law. The 'neueren Untersuchungen' are surely Fechner's 'Elemente der Psychophysik' (1860), which itself uses stellar magnitudes as evidence.

(c) Numerical analogue for sound. Divide sounds from ordinary loudness down to the threshold into eight 'magnitudes', with a factor 1/10 in intensity per magnitude:
- I_n/I_1 = 10^-(n-1);
- so I_2 = 1/10, I_3 = 1/100, ..., I_8 = 10^-7 ('den zehn Milliontel Theil').
Since A ∝ sqrt(I), A_n/A_1 = 10^-(n-1)/2. Hence magnitudes 1, 3, 5, 7 have amplitudes 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000. My consistency check: the p. 7 ratio 4·10^6 corresponds to log10(4·10^6) ≈ 6.6 magnitudes, i.e. about magnitude 7.6. This matches the claim that eight magnitudes span ordinary to barely audible.

(d) Middle-ear damping objection. Some authors assume strong sounds are damped, e.g. by reflex tension of the tympanic membrane through the tensor tympani. Riemann calls this arbitrary, with these points:
- protective reflexes may act against dangerous bangs;
- there is no auditory analogue of the eye's adaptation to illumination;
- a constantly varying reflex would be useless for following music.
The transfer ratio between air motion at the eardrum and stapes-footplate motion should therefore be the same at 10 ft and at 20,000 ft. Even if it varied, the conclusion would survive.

(e) Conclusion of I. Suppose stapes-footplate excursions at 10 ft are about the smallest visible to the naked eye. By the linear amplitude ratio 20,000/10 = 2000, excursions at 20,000 ft would be just visible at 2000× magnification. That is at or beyond the limit of microscopes of the time, which proves the p. 7 claim of 'more than microscopic' sensitivity.

(f) Start of thesis II, completed on p. 9. If such tiny motions are to be transmitted faithfully, the solid parts of the ossicular chain must fit together exactly at their contact points. A body cannot transmit motion to another from which it is separated by more than the amplitude.
errors: No arithmetical errors on this page.

Per-magnitude factor: the factor 1/10 in intensity per 'magnitude' is an arbitrary illustrative choice. The real stellar scale has a factor of about 2.512 (Pogson 1856), but Riemann only claims an analogy in form (geometric against arithmetic), so this is not an error.
Eighth magnitude versus p. 7: the eighth magnitude at 10^-7 is somewhat larger than the p. 7 ratio of 4·10^6 (about 6.6 magnitudes). This is acceptable given his 'etwa' and the rough distances.
Distance ratio: 20,000 ft / 10 ft = 2000 is an approximation to 4-5 miles (21,120-26,400 ft) against 8-10 ft (true range about 2100-3300). The approximation is conservative for his argument.
Inverse-square assumption: inverse-square propagation over water ('or faster') is assumed rather than demonstrated. It is plausible as a lower bound on attenuation.
Possible misprint on p. 7, not this page: '1 zu 1000 Millionen oder 1 zu Tausend' sits oddly with the computed 4 Millionen / 2000.

results.what: Analogy of loudness perception with stellar magnitude scale: physical intensity decreases geometrically while perceived magnitude increases arithmetically
results.modern_name: Weber–Fechner law (logarithmic sensation scale); stellar magnitude scale
results.usually_credited_to: E. H. Weber (1834), G. T. Fechner (1860); magnitudes as logarithmic: Steinheil, J. Herschel, Pogson (1856)

results.what: Eight 'sound magnitudes' with intensity factor 1/10 each, amplitudes scaling as square root of intensity (1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000 for magnitudes 1,3,5,7)
results.modern_name: Logarithmic loudness scale (proto-decibel/bel scale, 10 dB steps); amplitude ∝ sqrt(intensity)
results.usually_credited_to: Bel/decibel scale formalized by Bell Labs (1920s); the idea is Fechnerian

results.what: Estimate that stapes motions from just-audible sounds require about 2000× magnification to be seen, so the middle ear transmits sub-microscopic amplitudes; argument against level-dependent tympanic damping
results.modern_name: Hearing-threshold displacement amplitude estimate; linearity of middle-ear transfer
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann, 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867); later quantitative threshold estimates by Rayleigh (1877/1894) and Wien (1888)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed page of Riemann's known posthumous paper 'Mechanik des Ohres' (Henle & Pfeufer's Zeitschrift, 1867, and in his Werke). The content is an order-of-magnitude estimate plus an appeal to Fechner's law, both known as his and mathematically elementary. A logarithmic loudness scale in 10× intensity steps prefigures the bel, but that idea was already Fechnerian.

checkable.asserts: Eighth-magnitude sound has 1/10,000,000 the intensity of first magnitude with factor 1/10 per magnitude.

checkable.sympy: [sqrt(Rational(1,10)**(n-1)) for n in [1,3,5,7]] == [1, Rational(1,10), Rational(1,100), Rational(1,1000)]
checkable.asserts: Amplitude ratios for magnitudes 1,3,5,7 are 1 : 1/10 : 1/100 : 1/1000 since amplitude ∝ sqrt(intensity).
Distance ratio 2000 under inverse-square law gives intensity ratio four million (p. 7).
About 6.6 decades of intensity, i.e. about 6.6 'magnitudes' beyond the first; consistent with the 8-magnitude scale.
The linear amplitude ratio between 10 ft and 20,000 ft is 2000, hence 2000× magnification needed.
True distance ratios (about 2112 to 3300) bracket and exceed the conservative 2000 used.

transcription_corrections: The image is a printed proof sheet, not a manuscript. The '{+[+}' before 'in der Entfernung' is a handwritten editorial bracket mark in ink, not part of the text.
There is a pencil marginal annotation at left near 'nimmt, werden unsere Schlüsse' (looks like a number, e.g. '323'). It is not transcribed and is probably an archival foliation or page reference.
'1/10,000000' is printed exactly so (old digit grouping for 1/10,000,000). The transcription is otherwise accurate.
